title: Buckeye
name: Buckeye
metaDescription: Buckeye 1031 exchange advisory for owners of I-10 industrial land, master-planned retail pads, and converting agricultural parcels in the far West Valley.

sections.html: Buckeye covers more land area than almost any other municipality in the state, and most of it is still catching up to the growth headed its way. Master-planned subdivisions are eating into former cotton and alfalfa fields west of the White Tanks, and industrial development is spilling west along I-10 from Goodyear and the Phoenix-Goodyear Airport area. An owner exchanging out of Buckeye land is usually selling into that growth curve, not against it.

sections.heading: Rooftops, Retail, and Industrial All Chasing Each Other
sections.html:
Retail in Buckeye trails the rooftops closely, with power centers and grocery-anchored pads opening as new master-planned communities fill in. Industrial and distribution space is the bigger long-term story, pulled west along the I-10 corridor as Goodyear and West Valley sites get scarcer and more expensive. Agricultural parcels still working the land west of town increasingly trade for their future entitlement value rather than for row-crop income, and land banking by builders and industrial developers is common.

Some of the largest single-owner landholdings in the Valley still sit inside Buckeye's town limits, remnants of ranching and farming operations that predate the current growth wave, and those holdings often move in large blocks rather than as individually platted parcels.

sections.heading: Where Replacement Capital Tends to Land
sections.html:
Owners exchanging into Buckeye commonly look at:

  • I-10 industrial and distribution land or built product
  • Grocery-anchored retail pads inside new master-planned communities
  • Raw or partially entitled land held for future rooftops
  • Agricultural parcels priced for eventual conversion
  • Single-tenant retail pads at planned interchange corners

sections.heading: Pricing Land Off the General Plan Instead of Current Zoning Alone
sections.html: A parcel's current zoning in Buckeye often understates what it's actually worth, since land near a planned interchange or a designated growth corridor can carry a much higher future-use value than its as-zoned agricultural or rural designation suggests. A buyer should pull the town's general plan and any pending rezoning applications on file before pricing raw land off current use alone. Two adjacent parcels can carry very different values if only one falls inside a designated growth area on the general plan map.

sections.heading: Old Irrigation District Assessments Still Attach to the Land
sections.html:
Much of the land now converting to rooftops and industrial in Buckeye sat inside an irrigation district for decades, and those districts can carry recorded assessments or delivery obligations that survive a sale. A buyer should confirm with the title company whether any irrigation district lien or assessment attaches to a specific parcel before closing, since clearing it after the fact is a slower process than catching it up front.

Old field drainage and canal easements can also cut across a parcel in ways that don't always show up clearly on a standard survey, and a buyer planning to develop raw former farmland should have those easements located and reviewed before finalizing a site plan, since relocating an active drainage line after the fact adds real cost and delay.

sections.heading: Moving Fast in a Market Institutional Buyers Already Watch
sections.html: Developers and institutional land buyers already track Buckeye's growth corridors closely, and a listed parcel with real entitlement upside doesn't sit long. An owner running a 1031 exchange here should have candidates lined up before the relinquished sale closes and should build at least one backup property into the identification list, since competing directly against faster-moving institutional capital on a single target is a poor position to be in with the clock running. A broker who already tracks large landholder relationships in Buckeye can sometimes surface a parcel before it's formally marketed, which matters more here than in a submarket with a deeper listed inventory.

faqs.q: Is Buckeye mostly a residential market or does it have real commercial and industrial product?
faqs.a: Both are growing fast. Retail and industrial are following the new rooftops, with industrial spilling west along I-10 from Goodyear as sites there get scarcer and land prices climb closer to what Buckeye can still offer.

faqs.q: Why would raw land in Buckeye be worth more than its current zoning suggests?
faqs.a: Land near planned interchanges or designated growth corridors often carries future-use value well above its current agricultural or rural zoning. Check the town's general plan and any pending rezoning before pricing it off current use alone, since the gap between the two can be substantial.

faqs.q: Do old irrigation district obligations still matter on former farmland in Buckeye?
faqs.a: They can. Recorded assessments or delivery obligations from a former irrigation district sometimes survive a sale, so confirm status with the title company before closing rather than after.

faqs.q: Are large landholdings common in Buckeye, or is most land already subdivided?
faqs.a: Large single-owner blocks, often remnants of former ranching or farming operations, still make up a meaningful share of the town's undeveloped land. Those parcels frequently sell in large blocks rather than as individually platted lots.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange of Phoenix tell me whether my Buckeye land sale qualifies for a 1031 exchange?
faqs.a: No. That determination is made by the investor's qualified intermediary, CPA, or tax attorney. This service coordinates sourcing, timelines, and communication among those advisors.

faqs.q: Do old canal or drainage easements affect development on former Buckeye farmland?
faqs.a: They can. Field drainage and canal easements sometimes cut across a parcel without showing up clearly on a standard survey, so have them located and reviewed before finalizing a site plan on any former agricultural land, since relocating an active line mid-project adds real cost and can push a construction schedule back by months.
